hints: Think about what the Calvin cycle needs besides ATP and CO2 - it needs hydrogen and electrons to make a more energy-rich molecule.
Focus on the reduction step of the cycle - which 3-carbon acid is converted into which 3-carbon sugar using reduced NADP?
walkthrough:
Link light dependent to light independent**
Reduced NADP is made in the light dependent stage when NADP accepts hydrogen and electrons from the electron transport chain. It then diffuses into the stroma where the Calvin cycle happens and acts as a source of reducing power.

Pinpoint the reduction reaction**
In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide fixed to RuBP forms GP. ATP provides energy and reduced NADP provides hydrogen and electrons to reduce GP to TP. Oxidised NADP then returns to the light dependent stage to be reused.
Final answer: Reduced NADP reduces glycerate-3-phosphate (GP) to triose phosphate (TP).

hints: If DCPIP steals the hydrogen, no reduced NADP reaches the Calvin cycle - trace what happens to GP, then TP, then regeneration of RuBP.
walkthrough:
Follow the knock-on effect**
Without reduced NADP, GP cannot be reduced to TP. Less TP means less can be used to regenerate RuBP. RuBP continues to react with CO2 in carbon fixation, so its concentration falls because use exceeds replacement.
Final answer: RuBP concentration decreases as it is used up in carbon fixation but is not regenerated, since no TP is made without reduced NADP.

hints: Start with tube A - it contains chloroplasts but no blue DCPIP. What colour does fully decolourised tube B need to match?
Think about judging time by eye - why is a fixed standard kept under the same lamp more reliable than memory?
Now look at the stored beaker - what would happen if bench light reached the chloroplast-DCPIP mixture before the timed test starts?
Connect light to the Hill reaction - no light means no electron flow, so what does foil ensure about the starting colour for every wavelength?
walkthrough:
Why tube A is needed**
Tube B starts blue-green and becomes greener as blue DCPIP turns colourless. Judging full decolourisation by eye is subjective. Tube A contains only chloroplast suspension, which is the exact colour of a fully decolourised tube B, so it gives an objective end-point for comparison under the same light.

Why foil is needed**
The Hill reaction needs light to split water, release electrons and reduce DCPIP. If the stock beaker is left in the light, DCPIP would start to decolourise before timing begins. Wrapping in foil and using a foil lid blocks light, stops the light dependent reaction, and ensures every fresh tube B starts with the same blue colour for a fair test.

Final answer: Tube A provides a colour standard for comparison to judge the end-point when all DCPIP in B is reduced. Foil prevents light reaching the stored mixture, preventing the light dependent reaction and premature reduction / decolourisation of DCPIP, so all tests start with the same colour.

hints: Substitute the orange time of 45 s into the given formula $rate = 1000 / t$ and keep one decimal place like the table.
walkthrough:
Substitute and calculate**
For orange light, $t = 45 \text{ s}$. So $rate = 1000 / 45 = 22.222... = 22.2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ to one decimal place, matching the precision of the other values in Table 2.1.

hints: Scan the rate column in Table 2.1 - which colour and wavelength gives the highest rate and which gives the lowest rate?
Quote the key numbers to support the pattern - compare purple 27.0 and orange about 22.2 with green 2.1.
Recall which wavelengths chlorophyll absorbs well and which it reflects - why would green light drive almost no electron flow?
Think about what absorbed light does to chlorophyll - how does excitation link to splitting water and reducing DCPIP faster?
Remember the name for a plot of rate of photosynthesis against wavelength and the role of accessory pigments in broadening absorption.
walkthrough:
Describe the pattern with data**
Rate is fastest in purple light at 425 nm with $27.0 \text{ s}^{-1}$ and high in orange at 625 nm with $22.2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ and red at 675 nm with $20.0 \text{ s}^{-1}$. Rate is slowest in green light at 525 nm with only $2.1 \text{ s}^{-1}$. Shorter decolourisation time means faster Hill reaction.

Explain absorption**
This matches the absorption spectrum of photosynthetic pigments. Chlorophyll absorbs blue-violet and orange-red light strongly for photosynthesis but absorbs green light very poorly and reflects it, so green drives little electron flow.

Link light to DCPIP reduction**
Absorbed photons excite electrons in photosystems, triggering photolysis of water, electron transport and non-cyclic photophosphorylation. More excitation means more electrons and hydrogen to reduce DCPIP to colourless, so decolourisation is faster. Accessory pigments absorb extra wavelengths and pass energy to chlorophyll, broadening the action spectrum seen here.

Final answer: Highest rate in purple at 425 nm (27.0 s-1), lowest rate in green at 525 nm (2.1 s-1); orange and red also high. Chlorophyll absorbs purple/blue and orange/red well but absorbs green poorly. Absorbed light excites electrons, driving electron transport and non-cyclic photophosphorylation, reducing DCPIP faster; pattern follows action spectrum, with accessory pigments absorbing additional wavelengths.
